The December Check-Writing Ritual Now Costs You Money

Every December I do two things badly. I shop for my wife and daughter on the last Saturday before Christmas, elbowing through a mall packed with everyone else who planned poorly, and I write my charity checks in that same panicked week.

The shopping habit costs me dignity. Starting this year, the check habit costs money.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act rewrote the charitable deduction for 2026. Medscape’s Physicians and Taxes Report 2025 put the median marginal tax rate for doctors at 35%.

Pile student loans, a late start on retirement savings, and a short earning window on top of that rate, and a wasted deduction stings us harder than most people.

Below are the rules that changed, the strategies that still work, and seven moves to make before the year runs out.

Charitable gifts now count on Schedule A only above 0.5% of adjusted gross income. Take $100,000 of AGI: the floor is $500, and a $10,000 gift shrinks to a $9,500 deduction.

Physician incomes make the haircut bigger: a couple with $600,000 of AGI forfeits the first $3,000 they give (my arithmetic, not a sourced figure). That slice is usually gone for good.

Thomson Reuters’ Practitioner’s Tax Action Bulletin says the floor creates no carryover on its own, and the disallowed amount survives only when you already have a carryforward from blowing past the AGI percentage limits.

Then there’s the cap. Filers in the 37% bracket (taxable income above $768,700 on a joint return and $640,600 for singles in 2026) get 35 cents of tax benefit per deducted dollar. Schwab’s illustration: a $10,000 gift that once saved $3,700 now saves $3,500.

The mechanism is a “2/37” reduction applied to the lesser of your total itemized deductions or your income above the 37% threshold, so it trims mortgage interest and state taxes too, and it lands after the floor has taken its bite.

A couple with $600,000 of taxable income never touches this cap, a detail that goes missing when the “35 cents” headline travels alone.

Congress handed something back as well. The standard deduction rose to $32,200 for joint filers ($16,100 for singles), and non-itemizers can deduct up to $1,000 of cash gifts, or $2,000 on a joint return.

The fine print is strict: cash only, public charities only, nothing to a donor-advised fund or a private foundation. Residents, fellows, and attendings without a mortgage should grab it, since it asks for nothing beyond a receipt.

Each strategy below hinges on whether you itemize, and that answer changed for plenty of physicians this year. The cap on state and local tax deductions, stuck at $10,000 since 2018, sits at $40,400 for 2026.

High earners get less of it. Above $505,000 of modified AGI, the cap shrinks by 30 cents per extra dollar until it lands back at $10,000 once income reaches $606,333.

A couple at $560,000 keeps $23,900 of room, and at $600,000 they keep $11,900. Inside that band every additional dollar of income also erases 30 cents of deduction, which pushes the real marginal rate on those dollars well above the bracket printed in the tables.

The bigger cap expires, reverting to $10,000 in 2030. And physicians who own a practice taxed as an S corporation or partnership can ask whether their state offers a pass-through entity tax election, which lets the business pay the state income tax and deduct it outside the cap.

Deadlines vary by state, and some states penalize you for skipping estimated payments on the entity tax, so a January 1 start for 2027 can beat a rushed December election. (I practice in Florida, which has no personal income tax to route through an entity, so the election does nothing for me.)

You can run the test in ten minutes. Add your capped state and local taxes, your mortgage interest, and your planned gifts above the floor. If the total clears $32,200, you itemize.

If you hold appreciated stock in a taxable account, this is the easiest win on the list.

Say you own $10,000 of Apple bought for $4,000. Sell it and you owe 20% on the $6,000 gain, or $1,200, leaving $8,800 for the charity. Hand over the shares and the charity receives the full $10,000, you deduct $10,000, and nobody pays the tax. Most physicians in that bracket also owe the 3.8% net investment income tax, which lifts the real bill on the sale to $1,428.

Small charities often can’t accept a stock transfer. A donor-advised fund solves that by taking the shares, selling them tax-free, and sending cash grants to your church or your kid’s school.

Flip the logic for losers. Sell them, bank the loss against other gains, and give the cash, because donating a stock that’s underwater throws the loss away.

A donor-advised fund works like a charitable holding account. You contribute cash or stock, take the deduction that year, let the balance sit invested, and recommend grants to charities on your own schedule.

The large brokerage-affiliated sponsors make setup easy, and you name a successor to direct whatever remains after your death.

Before 2026 the appeal was bunching: stack two years of gifts into one, itemize that year, and take the standard deduction in the off year.

Picture a couple who gives $52,000 annually, which produces $312,000 of deductions over six years. Giving $104,000 every other year and claiming the $32,200 standard deduction in between produces $408,600. That’s $96,600 more deducted for identical dollars to identical charities.

(The example is simplified: no other itemized deductions, with the floor and cap ignored.)

The floor adds a second job. Give every year, and you pay the 0.5% toll every year, but bunch and you pay it half as often. For a couple with $600,000 of AGI giving $30,000 a year, that’s $18,000 of deductions lost over six years versus $9,000 with every-other-year funding (again, my illustration).

Bunching has a hole in it. If state taxes and mortgage interest already carry you past the standard deduction every year, the off-year standard deduction gains you nothing, and the floor savings are all that’s left.

Qualified charitable distributions send money straight from a traditional IRA to a charity. The 2026 limit is $111,000 per person, or $222,000 for a couple, and the gift counts toward the required minimum distributions that begin at 73.

Take a $300,000 RMD: a $111,000 QCD leaves tax owed on the remaining $189,000.

The biggest advantage gets too little airtime. A QCD stays out of your income entirely, so the 0.5% floor and the 35-cent cap never touch it, and it works whether you itemize or take the standard deduction. Because it lowers AGI, it can also help keep you under the income tiers that raise Medicare Part B and Part D premiums.

Meet two of our regulars (their numbers are illustrative).

Dr. Addams is a W-2 hospitalist in Texas. She and her husband report $420,000 of AGI, pay $14,000 in property tax and $12,000 in mortgage interest, and give $8,000 a year in cash. Her floor is $2,100, so itemizing would total $31,900, a hair under the standard deduction.

She takes the $32,200 plus the new $2,000, or $34,200 a year. Suppose she puts $14,000 into a donor-advised fund this December and gives $2,000 in cash directly next year. Her two-year deductions rise from $68,400 to $72,100.

That extra $3,700 is worth about $900 at her 24% rate, a pleasant bonus and nothing more. Her bigger win is funding the account with appreciated index fund shares.

Dr. Smart is a 1099 anesthesiologist in California. He and his wife report $700,000 of AGI, pay $30,000 of mortgage interest, and give $40,000 a year. Their income sits above $606,333, so the SALT deduction is back to $10,000, yet they itemize every year anyway.

Bunching saves them one $3,500 floor every two years and little else, and their taxable income stays under the 37% line, so the cap never bites.

The real money sits in two other places: donating stock to dodge a 23.8% federal tax on the gains, and a pass-through entity election that deducts California tax at his S corporation.

Late in the year partners start whispering about buyouts.

A physician selling in 2027 should plan to fund a donor-advised fund in the year the income spikes and start harvesting losses now to offset the coming gain. In a Roth conversion year, size stock gifts near 20% of projected AGI, which leaves room under the 30% limit because December income estimates are never exact.

Donating part of the practice itself before closing can work, and the Tax Court record shows how it fails. In Estate of Hoensheid v. Commissioner (2023), an owner gave shares to a donor-advised fund shortly before a sale that had become a practical certainty.

The court taxed him on the gain under the anticipatory assignment of income doctrine, then denied his deduction because the appraisal fell short of the rules. A gift like that has to happen when the deal can still fall apart, with a qualified appraisal in hand. State rules on who may own a medical practice add another barrier, so hire the attorney before you sign anything with a buyer.

Starting January 1, 2027, a federal credit of up to $1,700 applies to cash given to a scholarship granting organization that funds K-12 scholarships. A credit cuts your tax bill dollar for dollar, which beats a deduction worth 35 cents.

The catches matter. Your state has to opt in, the federal credit shrinks by any state credit you claim on that same gift, and you can’t deduct what you credit. If you already support a school scholarship fund, ask whether it qualifies before you write the 2027 check.

A word on what “by December 31” means. A check counts for 2026 if you mail it by December 31, and a credit card gift counts on the day of the charge, even when you pay the bill in January. Stock counts when the transfer completes, which is why brokers want instructions early.

December 31 is the legal deadline. The practical one arrives while you’re still eating leftover turkey, so call your CPA this week and save that last Saturday before Christmas for the mall.

This article is educational and is not tax, legal, or investment advice. Talk to your own CPA before acting.

#8555. The Busy Physician’s Black Friday Shopping Guide (2026): Smart Deals Without the Madness

Editorial Disclosure: Opinions, reviews, analyses & recommendations are the author’s alone, and have not been reviewed, endorsed, or approved by any of these entities.

Black Friday no longer fits in a single day. It now sprawls from early November through Cyber Monday, and every inbox, app, and billboard is shouting “lowest price ever” at the same time.

If you’re a physician, you don’t have the hours to sort real discounts from recycled list prices between clinic, call, charting, and a home life that also wants your attention.

So we did the sorting for you. This is not a shopping spree, and it’s not a detour from your FIRE plan. It’s a short list of deals on things busy physicians actually use: tech that saves time at work, gear for the home office and post-call recovery, kitchen tools that make weeknight meals easier, and a few upgrades that make hosting the holidays a lot less stressful.

The rule hasn’t changed since last year: if you need it, buy it well. If you don’t, keep the money and the mental bandwidth.

We cross-checked this year’s deals against Wirecutter, Wired, Forbes Vetted, and the New York Post, then checked every price on Amazon ourselves. We also brought back the picks Physician on FIRE readers actually bought from last year’s guide, wherever they’re discounted again.

Disclaimer: Prices and promotions change quickly, sometimes hourly, on Black Friday. Everything here was accurate when we published. Physician on FIRE may earn a commission on qualifying purchases made through links in this article, at no extra cost to you. Nothing here is an invitation to overspend or drift from your financially independent, retire early (FIRE) budget. We trust our readers to decide what’s right for them, whether that’s buying one thing on this list or nothing at all. (Please don’t buy everything.)

Tech is where Black Friday competition is fiercest, so it’s the best time to replace the earbuds that die halfway through your commute or finally put trackers on the things you keep losing.

Skip the shiny stuff and focus on gadgets that remove a daily annoyance.

Keys, call bag, badge lanyard, luggage. With AirTags attached, “where did I leave it” takes seconds instead of a frantic lap around the house before a 6 a.m. start. A reader favorite from last year’s guide. Buy on Amazon

See who’s at the door when you’re stuck in the OR, check that packages arrived, and keep an eye on the house from the hospital. This bundle was one of last year’s most-bought picks, and at 67% off it’s the deepest discount in this section. Buy on Amazon

The cheapest way to make a “dumb” house smart. Put the coffee maker, a lamp, or the holiday lights on a schedule, or turn them off from your phone when you realize mid-shift you left them on. Another proven reader pick. Buy on Amazon

A glare-free, warm-light screen for reading in the call room or in bed without the blue-light doomscroll. Wired names the Paperwhite the Kindle most people should buy, and this is a steep discount on it. Buy on Amazon

It snaps onto the back of an iPhone and fast-charges without a cable. Toss it in your white coat or call bag and stop hunting for an open outlet at the nurses’ station. Buy on Amazon

This is the deal every outlet we checked agreed on. Wired, Wirecutter, Forbes, and the Post all flagged it, and $149 is an outstanding price. The AirPods Pro 3 have excellent noise cancellation for the call room or a red-eye flight, a transparency mode clear enough for hallway conversations, built-in heart-rate tracking for workouts, and live translation that can help in a pinch with patients’ family members (it doesn’t replace a certified interpreter). If you’ve been nursing an older pair along, this is the time to upgrade. Buy on Amazon

Your workspace and your recovery between shifts deserve the same investment as your stethoscope. These are the picks that make charting, telehealth, and decompressing after call easier on your body.

Breathable mesh, adjustable lumbar support, and arms that actually adjust. It’s built for long evenings of charting and telehealth blocks. This was the most-clicked item in last year’s guide, and plenty of readers ended up buying one. Buy on Amazon

A sharp 4K screen means you can keep the EHR, imaging, and your inbox side by side without squinting. Wired calls it the monitor most people should buy, and it’s rarely been cheaper. Buy on Amazon

An affordable sit-stand desk with a spill-resistant top. Alternating between sitting and standing during admin time is one of the easiest ergonomic wins there is, and at this price it’s an easy yes. Buy on Amazon

A quiet, compact pedal machine that slides under your desk so you can move your legs while you finish notes or sit through a webinar. Wirecutter has it among its work-from-home deals. Buy on Amazon

Pocket-size percussive therapy for the neck, shoulders, and calves that hold onto every long case. It’s small enough to live in your locker or gym bag. Buy on Amazon

White noise, a wind-down routine, and a gradual sunrise alarm. It’s especially helpful when post-call sleep falls in the middle of the afternoon. Buy on Amazon

Shift work wrecks sleep, and most of us underestimate how much. The Oura Ring 5 tracks sleep stages, heart-rate variability, temperature trends, and recovery from a ring you’ll forget you’re wearing. It gives you hard data on what that string of nights actually costs you. Wired and Wirecutter both highlighted this deal, and it’s one of the few wearables on sale for a full $100 off. One note before you buy: Oura’s most detailed insights require a membership, so factor that into the total cost. Buy on Amazon

Healthy eating on a physician’s schedule comes down to two things: batch cooking on your day off, and making the rest of the week fast. These tools do both, and they’ll last long enough to justify the counter space.

The workhorse blender Wirecutter, Wired, and Forbes all put on their lists this year. Smoothies for the drive in, soups for the week, nut butters on a lazy Sunday. It’s built to run for a decade. Buy on Amazon

It air-fries, roasts, toasts, and dehydrates, and it’s big enough for a sheet-pan dinner or a 14-pound turkey. Think of it as a second oven for the holidays and a faster first oven for weeknights. Buy on Amazon

Made in France and practically indestructible. Braises, chili, sourdough, and holiday sides all come out better in enameled cast iron. This is one of the steepest discounts on the list for a buy-it-once piece. Buy on Amazon

Wireless probes report to your phone, so you can watch the roast while you greet guests. Hitting a safe internal temperature without hovering over the oven is a very physician-approved approach. Buy on Amazon

Onions, garlic, herbs, and pesto in seconds, without hauling out the full food processor. It’s small, quick to clean, and a Wirecutter deal pick. Buy on Amazon

Nesting bowls with lids double as meal-prep storage, so they go from mixing to the fridge without another dish to wash. Buy on Amazon

If coffee is what’s actually keeping your department running, this is the machine to own. The Moccamaster is handmade in the Netherlands and brews a full carafe at the right temperature in about six minutes. There’s no app or touchscreen to fail, and it has a five-year warranty, which is why it shows up as a top pick at Wirecutter and Wired year after year. The “Select” model adds a half-carafe setting for days when it’s just you. It’s a lot to spend on a coffee maker, but this deal makes it about as good a buy as it gets, and it should outlast a few residency classes. Buy on Amazon

Whether you’re hosting the whole family or just a few friends between shifts, these are the low-effort upgrades that make the house feel ready and make the cleanup afterward less painful.

The instant “the house smells like the holidays” fix. It’s warm and woodsy and throws enough scent for a big room, with up to 150 hours of burn time. It was one of last year’s reader favorites. Buy on Amazon

Red wine on the tablecloth, gravy on the couch, toddler mystery stains on the guest sheets. This was the No. 1 bestseller from last year’s guide, and it earns its spot under the sink every holiday season. Buy on Amazon

The cult-favorite spot cleaner for rugs, upholstery, and car seats. Pair it with the Miss Mouth’s spray and post-party spills stop being a crisis. Buy on Amazon

A long-running Wirecutter favorite that quietly clears a bedroom or living room of dust, pet dander, and cooking smoke. Useful for guests with allergies, and for anyone who’d like to dodge the house-wide winter cold. Buy on Amazon

Add or remove the shredded-foam fill until it fits your sleeper. It’s an easy way to make the guest room feel like a hotel, and it’s a Wirecutter deal pick this week. Buy on Amazon

For the couch, the guest room, or the in-law who’s always cold. It has adjustable heat settings and auto shut-off, and it’s machine washable once you unplug the controller. Buy on Amazon

The best thing you can buy for a household where nobody has time to vacuum. The Shark AI Ultra maps your home, cleans on a schedule while you’re at work, and empties itself into a bagless base that holds up to 30 days of debris. That covers the run-up to a holiday party and the cleanup afterward. Shark’s AI Ultra line was one of last year’s best sellers with POF readers, and at 53% off (a deal Forbes Vetted also flagged), it’s less than half its usual price. Run it daily and reclaim an hour a week for things that matter more. Buy on Amazon

Long shifts, N95s, hospital air, and too little sleep show up on your skin. These are simple, effective picks that fit a five-minute morning or a wind-down routine, plus a few stocking stuffers that don’t feel like an afterthought.

Smooth satin is gentler on hair and skin, with less frizz and fewer sleep creases on the face. At this price it’s an easy add-on, and it was the single most-ordered item from last year’s guide. Buy on Amazon

A kale-and-spinach gel cleanser that clears away sunscreen and the day’s grime without stripping your skin. Wirecutter has it on sale this week too. Buy on Amazon

An affordable, well-formulated vitamin C serum for morning brightening and antioxidant support under sunscreen. Both Forbes and Wirecutter flagged this deal. Buy on Amazon

Half off the countertop water flosser your dentist keeps mentioning. It’s faster than string floss and a real upgrade for anyone with crowns, implants, or braces in the family. Buy on Amazon

Forbes Vetted’s pick for the best whitening strips, at a good price ahead of holiday photos. Buy on Amazon

An overnight lip treatment that fixes dry, mask-chapped lips by morning. It’s the stocking stuffer everyone secretly wants. Buy on Amazon

Hands-free LED therapy that adds zero minutes to your routine. Put it on while you answer portal messages or decompress after a shift. Red and near-infrared light are popular for supporting collagen and calming irritated skin, and this mask covers both face and neck. It was a reader favorite last year, and it’s cheaper this time around. As always, keep expectations realistic: consistency matters more than intensity. Buy on Amazon

Some of the best gifts buy back time together: screen-free play for the kids, a way to keep grandparents in the loop, and one shared calendar to tame everyone’s schedule (call shifts included).

The magnetic building set that holds kids’ attention for years, not days. It’s a rare discount on a toy Wirecutter and the Post both recommend. Buy on Amazon

A four-foot floor puzzle that turns a rainy afternoon into a family project. It’s an inexpensive, reliable gift, and a quiet bestseller with readers last year. Buy on Amazon

A motion-tracking game console that gets kids (and parents) off the couch with no controllers needed. It’s one of this season’s most-recommended family gifts, and this is a strong discount. Buy on Amazon

A STEM marble run that teaches gravity and momentum through trial and error. It’s nearly half off and expands for years as kids get more ambitious. Buy on Amazon

A screen-free audio player for stories, music, and podcasts that kids control themselves with physical cards. It’s great for road trips, quiet time, and bedtime when you’re on call. Buy on Amazon

A wall-mounted touchscreen that syncs everyone’s calendars, chores, and meal plans in one place. If your call schedule is the reason the family keeps missing things, this is the fix. Buy on Amazon

Our favorite gift for parents and in-laws, and Wirecutter’s pick for the best digital frame. Set it up for them, then anyone in the family can send photos straight from their phone to the frame from anywhere, with unlimited free storage and no subscription. When you can’t make every visit, a steady stream of new photos of the kids on the grandparents’ counter is the next best thing. Buy on Amazon

Retailers count on urgency, not strategy. Plenty of “doorbusters” are engineered to look like a steal and end up as clutter (or e-waste) by February. A discount only matters if the product earns its place in your life.

Black Friday shopping doesn’t have to derail your financial plan or eat a day you don’t have. Everything on this list solves a real problem, lasts years rather than months, or buys back time. But value only counts if the purchase matches a need you already have.

If your coffee maker is dying, the Moccamaster is a great buy. If it works fine, keep the $248. If nobody in your house has vacuumed since September, the Shark will change your life. If you already have a routine that works, enjoy the savings by doing nothing at all.

The deals are real. The pressure to buy is manufactured.

Shop deliberately, and from everyone at Physician on FIRE, Happy Holidays!

Most of this year’s deals went live the week before Thanksgiving and run through Cyber Monday (November 30, 2026). Some Amazon prices change hourly, and popular items sell out, so if something on this list solves a real problem for you, don’t wait until Monday night.

Nearly every deal in this guide is available to all Amazon shoppers. Prime members sometimes get faster shipping or occasional member-only pricing. If you’re not a member, a free trial can cover holiday shipping. Just set a reminder to cancel if you don’t plan to keep it.

For electronics, small kitchen appliances, and home goods, Black Friday and Cyber Monday usually match or beat the year’s lowest prices. Inflated “list prices” do exist, though. We checked each item against current Amazon pricing and recommendations from Wirecutter, Wired, Forbes, and the New York Post. Price-history tools like CamelCamelCamel or Keepa can confirm a deal before you buy.

After Cyber Monday, the next big Amazon events are Prime Day (typically July) and Prime Big Deal Days (typically October). For most categories, though, the Thanksgiving-to-Cyber Monday window remains the year’s best chance at deep discounts.

From its humble beginnings in 2008 to today, Bitcoin’s history has been relatively short but very eventful. The original protocol for this popular digital currency was created in 2008 by Satoshi Nakamoto, believed to be a pseudonym for an unknown developer or group of developers.

Nakamoto launched the Bitcoin network just a year later and began mining the currency— an estimated 1 million bitcoins were mined in the early years.

The creator(s) of this first-of-its-kind asset developed the cryptocurrency in response to the Great Recession of 2007-2009, spurred by a distrust of the traditional banking system and concerns about its stability.

Given the recent values of Bitcoin, it’s hard to believe the currency first started trading on exchanges in 2010 at under $0.10. Since then, it’s experienced astronomical growth and some pretty wild price swings.

At its most recent high, one bitcoin was worth over $64,000—a far cry from trading for pennies in its earliest days.

Whether you’re thinking of investing in Bitcoin or you’ve held this cryptocurrency for several years, it’s fun to look back at this groundbreaking asset’s history. Read on for insights on Bitcoin milestones, historical returns, and how its returns compare to those of other assets.

Since being created, Bitcoin has experienced several milestones. Here’s a look back at some of the most significant moments in the short history of this cryptocurrency:

While Bitcoin isn’t exempt from the volatility cryptocurrencies often experience, it’s delivered some impressive returns over the years. Here’s a look at Bitcoin’s annual returns from 2010 to 2022:

And here’s a look at monthly returns, if you feel like getting a deeper dive:

While Bitcoin has experienced some wild monthly price swings and a couple of years where its value has declined, you can see that its declines have been eclipsed by some incredible gains. Now let’s explore how Bitcoin’s value has changed over 10, 5, 3, and 1 years.

Let’s say you bought one bitcoin on August, 3rd 2013, for $1,106.75, its price at the time. If you held that one bitcoin until August 3rd, 2023, it would’ve been worth $29,310.44, and your total ROI for the 10 years would be 2,546.8%.

We’ll also assume you purchased one Bitcoin for this example. A single bitcoin was valued at $965.31 on August, 3rd, 2018, and its value climbed to $29,310.44 by August 2023. Using our calculation above, your total ROI for those five years would be 294.1%.

A single bitcoin was valued at $11,246.20 in August 2020, and its value climbed to $29,310.44 at the end of 2021. Your total ROI for those three years would be 160.6%.

If you purchased a single bitcoin in August 2022, you would’ve paid around $22,626.83. In one year, that value would’ve increased to $29,310.44. Your total returns for that year would be 29.54%.

Instead of buying one bitcoin, let’s say you decided to invest $1,000 into Bitcoin. Here’s a look at how this $1,000 investment would’ve performed if you bought and held your Bitcoin for 10, 5, 3, and 1 years.

While Bitcoin’s earliest investors would have benefitted the most from buying and holding their Bitcoin, those who’ve invested recently also fared well.

If you’re curious how Bitcoin returns compare to those of other asset classes, here’s how its annual and total returns compare to gold, real estate, and the S&P 500.(Spoiler alert: Bitcoin outperformed all three assets by an enormous margin.)

If you compare Bitcoin’s returns to gold’s returns, you’ll notice a stark difference. Bitcoin has an average annual return of 1,576% and a total return of 18,912% from 2010 to 2022, while SPDR Gold Shares had an average annual return of just 5.14% and a total return of 61.67% over the same period.

Let’s see if real estate fared any better compared to Bitcoin. The cryptocurrency delivered a whopping 1,576% average annual return and an 18,912% total return from 2010 to 2021, while the Vanguard Real Estate ETF had an average annual return of 13.49% and a total return of 161.91% over the same period.

So, real estate saw slightly higher returns than gold, but it still didn’t come close to Bitcoin’s returns.

The S&P 500 didn’t fare too much better in its head-to-head with Bitcoin. From 2011 to 2023, the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF delivered an average annual return of 15.74% and a total return of 173.14%. While those numbers aren’t too shabby, Bitcoin’s average annual return for the same period was a whopping 819%, and its total return was 9,012%.

We’ve analyzed how Bitcoin compares to gold, real estate, and the stock market, but how does it stack up against some of the best-performing stocks? Here’s how this popular cryptocurrency stacks up against major companies like Amazon, Apple, Berkshire Hathaway, JP Morgan, Microsoft, Visa, and Walmart.

We looked at the average annual and total returns for each asset. This data assumes you bought the asset in 2010 and held it until 2023.

While some investors may be skeptical about cryptocurrency, citing concerns over market volatility and a high risk of loss, Bitcoin’s performance over time paints a rosy picture. With its longevity and astronomically high returns, Bitcoin has been worth the risk for many investors—especially early adopters.

Of course, historical performance doesn’t guarantee future returns. So if you’re considering investing in cryptocurrency, only invest what you can afford to lose.

#8551. Shop Your House Before Buying School Supplies – What You Reuse Beats Any Sale

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Before you buy school supplies, gather last year’s leftovers, from backpacks and binders to calculators and pens, and cross everything that still works off the teacher’s list. Then buy only what’s still missing, and get the basics during July’s back-to-school sales, when folders, notebooks, and crayons can cost under a dollar each.

A leftover you reuse costs nothing this year, so it beats even back-to-school sale prices. And the priciest things a list asks for, like a backpack, a binder, or a calculator, usually outlast the school year.

Families with kids in elementary through high school planned to spend an average of $146.45 on school supplies in 2026, according to the National Retail Federation’s annual back-to-school survey. Say two kids’ lists come to $120 at regular prices, and two backpacks and a calculator make up $60 of it. Reuse those three, buy the other $60 of supplies on July’s deals for about $40, and the year’s supplies cost $40 instead of $120. Three-quarters of that $80 saving comes from the backpacks and calculator you didn’t buy.

Start with the house. Empty last year’s backpacks, desk drawers, and pencil boxes, test every marker and glue stick, check zippers and straps, and write down what still works.

Then wait for the teacher’s list and buy only what it asks for, in plain versions rather than character-branded ones your child may outgrow by next year. If the list won’t arrive until the first week of school, buy pencils and notebooks in July and leave anything specific, like a binder size or a calculator model, until it does.

Buy the basics in July, when office supply chains sell 2-pocket folders for 25 cents and boxes of crayons for 50 cents, often with a limit per customer. For a calculator or another item the list names by model, Staples and Office Depot will match another store’s lower price, though each excludes some sales. For supplies every child uses up, like pencils and glue sticks, a warehouse club’s bulk pack can cover all your kids. First compare its unit price, the price per item, with what each item costs on sale in July. Save the pricier items still on the list for your state’s sales tax holiday, if it has one.

When school lets out, put whatever survived the year in one bin, and open it before you shop next summer.

#8550. Retired Man Tries to Spend More Money, Mostly Fails

A couple of years ago, Mr. Money Mustache lost some credibility among the faithful when he wrote this blog post about actually trying to spend a bit more money, while buying a Tesla as the first step in that program.

“I’m such an enlightened middle-aged Badass, adjusting habits and realigning myself at the snap of my fingers. Onward to the next forty eight years of the Good Life!”

So, two years passed with an even greater feeling of abundance. I had a marvelous time traveling everywhere and spending money like I thought a proper wealthy person would do.

I dined out in stylish restaurants, booked hotels based on their niceness rather than their cheapness, paid extra to sit in the “reduced torture” seats of the airplanes, and gave zero fucks about paying double for groceries if I happened to be in a Whole Foods rather than my usual Sam’s Club and Costco (and yes I treat myself to memberships at both warehouse stores!)

Among the highlights, my son and I have worked our way though a nice selection of late night EDM concerts and three Meowwolf art venues including a Christmas Day road trip from our winter home in Tempe Arizona to Las Vegas last year. And having spent much of the year as a single man, I had a wide open schedule to just meet up with friends, explore new places and meet new people as opportunities came up. It felt like a year of adventurous transition, which means it felt like much more than twelve months.

With all this flashy spending, I was sure my budget must have crept back into full American Consumer territory. But I was having too much fun to bother adding it all up to check.

Until recently, when I was doing another round of informal coaching for a friend and we both decided to tally our spending for the past year to compare notes.

When I finally finished sorting all of those transactions into a spreadsheet and hit the “sum” button, the results surprised me.

While my overall spending had indeed increased (especially in travel-related categories), the big-picture effect was still pretty minimal. Depending on how I account for things like the car and my business expenses, my spending went from $20,000 to about $30,000 (plus the usual hidden subsidy of a paid-off house.)

This level could still be sustained by a $1 million investment nest egg. Since my investments are quite a bit higher than that (especially after these recent years of crazy economic growth and the never-ending stock market rally), I’m still way under budget.

Although I still “failed” to really increase my spending to the MMM-recommended levels for old wealthy people, this still makes me happy, because I have genuinely had more fun with the abundance mindset, and I can keep trying more life experiments in the coming years.

As we covered in the 2019 article on the idea of an Optimization Council, it’s always a good idea to compare our spending, tips and tricks on how to get the most out of life. Almost twenty years into early retirement, this is where I have landed so far, although I’m always learning and open to feedback.

Anyway, let’s cut the wistful commentary and get into the budget.

In summary: Wow, how interesting! When we compare this to my 2019 post on that year’s spending, it’s only a bit higher even after all the inflation we have seen in recent years. I spent more on travel and fun, but less on home renovation – partly because I was away so much I didn’t have as much time to work on my house. The health insurance is a new cost too since I was self-insured back then.

My budget is notably missing the biggest expense for most people, which is housing costs. This is because I paid off my house long ago, and I also love working on and taking care of my own home, which means there are no bills for lawn mowing, plumbers, tree pruning or handyman services.

This strategy is not for everyone, and it’s not even the optimum financial one for me – I would have been better off taking out the biggest mortgage I could get at 3% back in the sweet borrowing times of 2021, and putting all that principal to work in stock index funds where it would have almost doubled since then. But I still get a great peace of mind from just having no mortgage payment, and there’s really no better way to use your money than to buy such good feelings. Also, I get a secondary benefit of not having to buy house insurance, which saves me another $2000 per year, boosting my effective return on that payoff.

First of all, the biggest money saving factor of good health and good luck has continued, meaning I’ve still had no actual medical expenses. But I still do maintain two layers of health care support which together feel very much like the ultimate version of health insurance: a membership with a top of the line Direct Primary Care (DPC) medical clinic ($107 per month) plus a high-deductible plan ($201) with a health sharing organization called Sedera.

The combined cost of $308 per month is less than the cheapest Bronze plan in the field of standard health insurance, yet I get personalized support with zero deductible for almost all typical medical needs, plus some protection from larger medical bills if my good luck runs out.

But as a disclaimer, I’m not an expert on medical needs and health insurance because I’ve had so little experience with the system. And the highest priority in my life is arranging my days for maximum health to give me the best chance of keeping it this way.

When it comes down to it, money is a tool for survival and if we’re lucky, self actualization. So I’m always asking myself if there’s anything I can change or improve to make the most of this good fortune.

I also try to keep in mind an interesting principle of happiness, which says that,

Fixing your persistent problems is more effective than just doubling down on things that are already good in your life.

For me, there are already a lot of good things which don’t need improving. My family, friends, relationships, health, food and daily activities are pretty much as good as I could imagine.

The only annoyance I can think of is physical chaos: I have a lot of space-intensive hobbies like construction and music, and I currently live in a pretty small house which is basically maxed out.  I could really use a doubling of my workshop space from the current 2-car, 440 square foot garage to maybe a thousand or so.

But I also love where I live and wouldn’t want to give up my views, neighbors or current place. So I’ll keep optimizing what I’ve got unless some perfect opportunity comes up for a bigger place right on my block.

In the longer run, a mountain compound with its own cliffs and stream are also on my “maybe” list. But once again, my days and life are already overbooked with joyful things. My existing house and our HQ Coworking space already have long to-do lists. Would I actually be happier if I added another place to my portfolio? So I keep this idea on the shelf until I’m willing to trade it for another existing commitment – like selling my house or the coworking space.

But for now, I’m just extremely excited to blaze into 2025 with loads abundance and piles of challenging stuff on my to-do list. And I wish you the same!

In the Comments: Where are you at on this spectrum of stinginess versus abundance mentality, and fulfilment versus longing in life?

Mr. Money Mustache January 17, 2025, 9:41 am

My boy is almost grown up now (turning nineteen this month!) but those expenses were indeed higher during certain parts of his childhood.

We never had mandatory childcare because both parents retired before he was born – specifically so we could both team up as stay at home parents. But we still paid for part time preschool to get him out in the world mingling with other kids, and it paid off in friendships for both him and for us to this day.

I think that it’s totally worth spending money on things that your kid wants to do. But drawing the line short of forcing them into being on multiple sports teams just because you think it would be food for them. And prioritizing local things so you’re not spending multiple hours in the car every week.

Kids benefit from lots of self-directed play time with their siblings and parents and friends in nature, and many organized activities take them directly away from this. So, a middle ground between the standard rich suburbanite lifestyle and the traditional village upbringing could be ideal.

This is a very good point. I am a retired insurance regulatory lawyer, and homeowners insurance just covers much more than the house. It covers YOU for liability. If you get sued, it also hires a lawyer to defend you and pays any judgement against you up to the policy limits. This is a great question and conversation starter. I retired early about two years ago, and I’m early in the process of considering these big ideas. I think a lot about how to do the most I can for my community without turning over 100% of my time to somebody else’s goals and whims.

A couple of core principles that I’m drawn to:

1. It’s all about the 80/20 rule — what are the 20% of actions we can take that will make 80% of the change? Pick one thing that aligns with your skills, interests, and influence, and work on that. For MMM, it’s reducing car traffic (and thereby carbon emissions) by persuading people to design their lives around biking. For me, it’s increasing literacy, particularly media literacy. I think if Americans were better able to distinguish propaganda, scams, etc. from good information, we would be much more effective at creating policies that benefit as many people as possible.

2. Giving money can be just as good (or better!!) than giving your time. I completely get MMM’s point here that it’s counterproductive to be locked into running a nonprofit full-time if that’s not how you work best. I believe people who prefer more time freedom can feel great about “just” providing funding for others who find meaning in devoting a lot of time to hands-on work. (And many people, like me, will fall in the middle, with some part-time volunteering and some donating.)

Many of us worry about problems that we have no real expertise in or direct control over, like preventing wildfires. It is a huge contribution to donate money strategically to the people who do have the expertise and the control, even if your time is going only to making art, enjoying nature, hanging out with friends, etc. We learned from MMM that our money works harder than us, and that can apply to charitable giving too!

I’ve benefited from the EV tax credit, but at the same time I don’t like the federal government distorting the market, but then also at the same time the federal government already does that in so many areas with ridiculous Byzantine regulations, so the EV tax credit could be seen as a form of “un-distortion”. Either way, if the tax credit disappears I am quite confident that the market will find a new equilibrium all on its own.

I’ve heard that “subsidy/distorted market” argument about EVs so many times over the past few years, and yet I find it mostly irrelevant. I think most people don’t know that the combustion engine vehicles industry has been heavily subsidized for decades, either through tax breaks, direct investments from the government, direct subsidies to oil companies and, in a more subtle way, by very lax environmental regulations that have allowed the production of these vehicles (or oil) at a distorted cost. The only difference is that when buying EVs, consumers receive the tax credit directly instead of getting a hidden discount on a combustion engine vehicle that was subsidized on the production line. So yes, in the end, everything is subsidized in one way or another!

MMM (or others), can you elaborate on the comment, “(plus the usual hidden subsidy of a paid-off house)”….exactly what is that? I think I am fairly informed in the world of finance (have been FIREd since 2014 @ age of 40) but not exactly sure what this is. Thank you!

It is a “subsidy” in the sense that it reduces monthly/yearly cash requirements by the amount of principal+interest (and in the case of MMM, insurance since he chooses to self-insure). If you have a mortgage then you have a requirement to pay the mortgage every month (PITI), but in MMM’s case he only pays the ‘T’ part or taxes.

If he had a mortgage, then his $30k/year spend would probably be closer to $60k/year (or something, depending on the amount financed, interest rates, insurance, etc.). So the subsidy is the reduction in annual spending because of not having the mortgage. But he got that by working at paying off the mortgage earlier in life, which he acknowledges is a trade off.

#8549. Kids Eat Free at 10 Chain Restaurants – Each Deal’s Day, Age Cutoff & Catch

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Several family chains let kids eat free one or two days a week, usually with one free kids’ meal for each paying adult entrée, and a couple let young kids eat free any day. Plan your family dinners out around those days, and confirm your location runs the deal before you go.

At Luby’s, where a kids’ meal costs $6.49, two adults with two kids 10 or younger who eat there on a kids-eat-free day pay only for their own meals and save $12.98. Four such dinners a month save $51.92.

Most of these deals work the same way. Each paying adult entrée earns one free kids’ meal for a child at or under an age cutoff, usually 10 to 12. Several chains also count only meals eaten in the restaurant.

That one-for-one ratio is the catch for bigger families. Two adults with three kids still pay for one kids’ meal, and some chains cap the free meals per table or per check instead of per adult.

These eight chains run their deals on set days of the week, listed from Tuesday on.

These two chains let young kids eat free every day of the week.

Some buffets also price kids’ meals by age. At the Pizza Ranch in Ames, Iowa, kids 1 to 12 pay $1.09 for each year of age, so a 6-year-old’s buffet costs $6.54.

On days without a deal, ordering water and sharing plates keeps the kids’ share of the bill low, and restaurant apps and birthday clubs give out free meals of their own.

Not every restaurant in a chain runs its deal. Red Robin, Smashburger, and Dickey’s limit theirs to participating locations, and Pizza Ranch’s age cutoffs and hours vary by location.

Smashburger and Dickey’s won’t combine their deals with any other offer, and Red Robin won’t combine its deal with its rewards, so save a coupon or reward for another visit. Ask whether the free kids’ meal includes a drink.

Pick the day that fits your week, then call the restaurant that day to confirm it’s running the deal and how many free kids’ meals your table gets.

When I became an accredited investor, I found myself among an elite group with the financial means and regulatory clearance to access investments that many couldn’t. This opened doors to exclusive realms like hedge funds, venture capital firms, specific investment funds, private equity funds, and more.

Even though I had this “exclusive access” it took me a while to start investing in alternative asset classes.

The Securities and Exchange Commission states that as an accredited investor, I possess a level of sophistication that equips me to craft a riskier investment portfolio than a non-accredited investor. While this might not be universally true for everyone, in my case, I had demonstrated the financial resilience to bear more risk (see barbell investing), especially if my investments took an unforeseen downturn.

One of the intriguing aspects I discovered was that investment opportunities for accredited investors aren’t mandated to register with financial authorities. This means they often come with fewer disclosures and might not be as transparent as the registered securities available to the general public.

The underlying belief is that my status as a sophisticated investor implies a deeper understanding of financial risks, a need for less disclosure of unregistered securities, and a conviction that these exclusive investment opportunities are apt for my funds.

On a personal note, as a practicing CFP®, I haven’t always worked with accredited investors. Early in my career, I didn’t quite grasp the allure. However, as time went on, I began to see the broader spectrum of investment options available to accredited investors.

As I learned more the clearer it became why this realm was so sought after. The variety and potential of these exclusive opportunities were truly eye-opening, reshaping my perspective on the world of investing.

An accredited investor is an individual or a business entity that is allowed to trade securities that may not be registered with financial authorities. They are entitled to this privileged access because they satisfy one or more requirements regarding income, net worth, asset size, governance status, or professional experience.

The concept of an accredited investor originated from the idea that individuals or entities with a higher financial acumen or more resources are better equipped to understand and bear the risks of certain investment opportunities.

Historically, the distinction between accredited and non-accredited investors was established to protect less experienced investors from potentially risky or less transparent investment opportunities.

Regulatory bodies, such as the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), have set criteria to determine who qualifies as an accredited investor, ensuring that they have the financial stability and sophistication to engage in more complex investment ventures.

To be classified as an accredited investor, one must meet specific criteria set by regulatory bodies:

Here’s a rundown of some of the top investments for accredited investors…

Fundrise has revolutionized the real estate investment landscape. By democratizing access to real estate portfolios, it allows individuals to invest without the complexities of property management or the need for vast capital. The platform’s innovative approach provides exposure to a traditionally lucrative, yet often inaccessible, sector of the market

Through Fundrise, investors can access a diversified range of properties, from commercial ventures to residential units. The platform’s expert team curates these portfolios, ensuring a balance of risk and reward. With its user-friendly interface and transparent reporting, Fundrise has become a top choice for many venturing into real estate investments.

Investors start by choosing a suitable investment plan on Fundrise. Once invested, the platform pools the funds with other investors and allocates them across various real estate projects. As these properties generate rental income or appreciation in value, investors receive returns in the form of dividends or appreciation.

Equitybee offers a unique platform that bridges the gap between private companies on the cusp of going public and potential investors. This innovative approach provides a golden opportunity for investors to tap into the potential of startups and other private firms before they make their public debut.

The platform’s primary focus is on employee stock options. By allowing investors to invest in these options, they can potentially benefit from their appreciation as the company grows. With a vast array of companies, from emerging startups to established giants, Equitybee presents a diverse range of investment opportunities.

Investors browse available stock options from various companies on Equitybee. Once they choose an option, they invest their funds, which are then used to purchase the stock options from the employees. If the company goes public or gets acquired, the investor stands to gain from the increased value of these stocks.

Percent stands as a beacon in the vast sea of the private credit market, illuminating a sector often overshadowed by traditional investments. This burgeoning market, valued at over $7 trillion, consists of companies borrowing from non-bank lenders. Percent offers a unique vantage point into this market, allowing investors to diversify their portfolios beyond typical stocks and bonds.

The allure of Percent lies in its ability to offer shorter terms and higher yields, combined with investments that are largely uncorrelated with public markets. This makes it an attractive proposition for those looking to step away from the volatility of traditional markets.

Upon joining Percent, investors are presented with a plethora of private credit opportunities. After selecting an investment, funds are pooled with other investors and lent out to companies seeking credit. As these companies repay their loans, investors earn interest, providing a steady income stream.

Masterworks paints a vivid picture of art investment, blending the worlds of finance and fine art. Traditionally, investing in art was a luxury reserved for the elite. However, Masterworks has democratized this, allowing individuals to buy shares in artworks from world-renowned artists.

The platform’s strength lies in its expertise. From authentication to storage, every facet of art investment is handled meticulously. This ensures that investors can appreciate both the beauty of their investments and the potential financial returns.

After registering on Masterworks, investors can browse a curated selection of artworks. They can then purchase shares, representing a fraction of the artwork’s value. Masterworks take care of storage, insurance, and eventual sale. When the artwork is sold, investors share the profits based on their ownership.

Yieldstreet stands at the intersection of innovation and alternative investments. It offers a smorgasbord of unique investment opportunities, ranging from art to marine finance. For those looking to venture beyond the beaten path of traditional stocks and bonds, Yieldstreet presents a tantalizing array of options.

The platform’s allure lies in its curated selection of alternative investments, each vetted by experts. This ensures that while investors are treading unconventional grounds, they’re not stepping into the unknown blindly.

Investors begin by browsing through the diverse investment opportunities on Yieldstreet. After selecting their preferred asset class, their funds are pooled with other investors and allocated to the chosen venture. Returns are generated based on the performance of these assets, be it through interest, dividends, or asset appreciation.

AcreTrader, as its name suggests, brings the vast expanses of farmland to the investment table. It offers a unique opportunity to invest in agricultural land, combining the stability of real estate with the evergreen nature of agriculture. With the global population on the rise, the value of fertile land is only set to increase.

The platform meticulously vets each piece of land, ensuring only the most promising plots are available for investment. This rigorous process ensures that investors are planting their funds in fertile ground, poised for growth.

Investors peruse available farmland listings on AcreTrader. After selecting a plot, they can invest, effectively owning a portion of that land. AcreTrader manages all aspects, from liaising with farmers to ensuring optimal land use. Investors earn from the appreciation of land value and potential rental income.

EquityMultiple is a testament to the power of collective investment in the real estate sector. By leveraging the principles of crowdfunding, it offers a platform where multiple investors can pool their resources to finance high-quality real estate projects. This collaborative approach allows for diversification and access to projects that might be out of reach for individual investors.

The platform’s strength lies in its curated selection of real estate opportunities, ranging from commercial spaces to residential properties. With a team of seasoned real estate professionals at the helm, EquityMultiple ensures that each project is vetted for maximum potential and minimal risk.

Upon joining, investors can explore a variety of real estate projects. After committing to a project, their funds are pooled with other investors to finance the venture. Returns are generated through rental incomes, property appreciation, or the successful completion of development projects.

CrowdStreet stands as a pillar in the commercial real estate investment domain. With its vast experience and industry connections, it offers a platform where investors can tap into prime real estate projects across the nation. From bustling urban centers to tranquil suburban locales, CrowdStreet provides a diverse range of investment opportunities.

The platform’s expertise ensures that each project is meticulously vetted, offering a blend of potential returns and stability. For investors looking to delve into commercial real estate without the hassles of property management, CrowdStreet is an ideal choice.

After registration, investors can browse a myriad of commercial real estate offerings. Upon investing in a project, CrowdStreet manages the investment, providing regular updates and ensuring optimal project execution. Investors earn returns based on the project’s performance, be it through rentals, sales, or project completions.

Mainvest offers a refreshing twist in the investment landscape, focusing on the heart and soul of the American economy: local businesses. From quaint cafes to innovative startups, Mainvest provides a platform where investors can support and benefit from the growth of small businesses in their communities.

The platform’s community-centric approach ensures that investments are not just about returns but also about fostering local economies. For those looking to make a difference while earning, Mainvest presents a unique opportunity.

Investors can explore various local businesses seeking capital on Mainvest. By investing, they essentially buy a revenue-sharing note, earning a percentage of the business’s gross revenue until a predetermined return is achieved.

Vinovest uncorks the world of wine investment, offering a blend of luxury, history, and financial growth. Fine wines have been a symbol of opulence for centuries, and Vinovest provides a platform where this luxury becomes an accessible investment.

With a team of wine experts guiding the way, the platform ensures that each wine is not just a drink but an investment poised for appreciation. From sourcing to storage, Vinovest handles every facet, ensuring the wine’s value grows over time.

After signing up, investors set their preferences and investment amounts. Vinovest then curates a wine portfolio based on these preferences, handling sourcing, authentication, and storage. As the wine appreciates, so does the investor’s portfolio.

Arrived Homes offers a fresh perspective on real estate investment, focusing on the charm of single-family homes. While skyscrapers and commercial complexes often dominate real estate discussions, single-family homes offer stability, consistent returns, and a touch of nostalgia.

The platform’s strength lies in its focus. By concentrating on single-family homes, it offers investors a chance to tap into a stable real estate segment, benefiting from both rental income and property appreciation.

Investors browse available properties on Arrived Homes. After selecting a property, they can invest in shares, representing a portion of the home’s value. As the property is rented out, investors earn a share of the rental income. Additionally, any appreciation in property value benefits the investors.

RealtyMogul stands tall in the commercial real estate investment landscape. It offers a platform where diversification meets opportunity, presenting a range of commercial properties for investment. From bustling office spaces to serene residential complexes, RealtyMogul provides a plethora of options for investors to expand their portfolios.

The platform’s prowess lies in its dual approach. Investors can either dive into non-traded REITs or make direct investments in specific properties. This flexibility ensures that both novice and experienced investors find opportunities that align with their investment goals.

Upon joining RealtyMogul, investors can choose between REITs or direct property investments. Their funds are then channeled into these real estate ventures. Returns are generated through rental incomes, property sales, or successful project completions.

The world of accredited investing is dynamic and ever-evolving. Emerging trends suggest a shift towards democratizing investment opportunities, with regulatory bodies considering more inclusive criteria for accredited investor status. This shift aims to balance the need for investor protection with the recognition that financial acumen can come from experience and education, not just wealth.

Furthermore, technological advancements are playing a pivotal role. The rise of blockchain and tokenized assets, for instance, is creating new avenues for investment and might reshape the landscape of opportunities available to accredited investors.

As the line between traditional and alternative investments blurs, the future promises a more integrated, inclusive, and innovative environment for accredited investors.

Understanding the role and opportunities of accredited investors is crucial in the modern financial landscape. While the distinction offers privileged access to unique investment opportunities, it also comes with increased risks and responsibilities.

As the world of investing continues to evolve, potential accredited investors are encouraged to stay informed, conduct thorough research, and seek professional advice. The realm of accredited investing, with its blend of challenges and opportunities, promises exciting prospects for those ready to navigate its complexities.

If you keep making the same money mistake despite knowing better, work on the thought that sets the habit off. Cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT, teaches you to catch and test it, and a financial therapist pairs that work with money coaching. Start with a free self-help workbook, or ask your health plan for a CBT therapist.

A money mistake you keep repeating starts with a thought that goes by fast, like “it’s all bad news anyway” when a bill arrives or “I deserve this” at the checkout. By the time you notice it, the envelope is in a drawer or the purchase is made.

Cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT, works on that thought, whether it leads to overspending, unopened bills, or a decision you keep putting off. A therapist teaches you to spot it, test it against the facts, and practice a different response, with homework between sessions. The American Psychological Association reports that CBT has been shown to work for depression and anxiety disorders, and in many studies it has matched or beaten other talk therapies and psychiatric medication.

Picture someone who leaves mail unopened for weeks and pays a late fee most months. Over eight sessions, he learns to catch the thought that it’s all bad news anyway, and he sets a 10-minute mail routine every Sunday. The late fees stop.

Start on your own. The Centre for Clinical Interventions, a service of Western Australia’s Department of Health, offers free self-help workbooks, including one on procrastination that has you identify and test the excuses behind putting things off. For a habit with no worry behind it, like nightly takeout, swap in a cheaper routine that gives a similar reward.

A financial therapist combines work on your feelings about money with coaching on the money itself, so pick one when you want help with both. A financial planner works on goals such as retirement, and a credit counselor on your budget and debts.

Financial therapy isn’t regulated in the U.S., so confirm that anyone you find in the Financial Therapy Association’s directory holds a mental health license or the association’s Certified Financial Therapist credential, CFT-I. For CBT, the Association for Behavioral and Cognitive Therapies lists licensed therapists you can search by zip code.

Most individual and small-employer health plans must cover mental health care. Call the member services number on your insurance card and ask which therapists in your plan’s network use CBT.
